peak_relief.c: BC Hydro: Demand Response for Business $50/kW-season, events ≤4 h, Nov–Mar, diesel and fossil generators prohibited; Energy Storage Incentive ≤80 % of eligible cost, new non-exporting batteries ≥25 kW, 10-yr contract (an existing UPS does not qualify); LGS demand charge $13.83/kW·month; AESO reserves need ≥5 MW (supplemental) or ≥10 MW (spinning), smaller sites via an aggregator | 19 Oct 2026: ESI pays up to 80% of eligible cost (LGS, ≥25 kW, non-exporting, 10-yr); AESO reserve averages per …

genset_test.f: energy = units × kW × test hours at load; × emission factors
genset_test.c: testing ≈14.5 h/yr per unit, ~4 h at full load (AUC 27938-D01-2023, Amazon 25.6 MW, derived); Vancouver noise by-law exemption caps tests ≈15 h/yr; uncontrolled diesel 14.6 g NOx, 0.43 g PM, 706 g CO2 per kWh (AP-42 Table 3.4-1, upper bound for modern engines); Alberta exempts standby generators from environmental approval

hvo_swap.f: Δ lifecycle CO2e = fuel energy × (CI diesel − CI renewable diesel)
hvo_swap.c: BC approved fuel codes −7 to 131 g CO2e/MJ (RLCF-012, Apr 2026); stack CO2, NOx and PM stay about the same; fossil diesel reference CI to retrieve

borefield.n: Borefield as the data centre's heat sink
borefield.f: L = heat to ground (W) ÷ q; boreholes = L ÷ 150 m; area = boreholes × 36 m²
borefield.c: q = 12 W/m (base design, 1,248 m) to 19 W/m (economic optimum, about 760 m), both for the ground-only heat-pump system; the dry-cooler hybrid only reused 760 m (derived by dividing the 14.5 kW cooling load by length, not the heat rejected to the ground, which also includes compressor work; Zurmuhl et al. 2018 s. 3.1, 4.2.1–4.2.2, a 14.5 kW data centre, Ithaca, k 3.27 W/m·K; checked 18 Oct 2026); Edmonton design k 1.9 W/m·K (Alberta Geological Survey) → ~7–11 W/m (scaling is an assumption); ≈2 …
borefield.st: screening; no standard for continuous rejection

ground_warming.f: from the share of heat put in vs taken out
ground_warming.c: +4.7 K over 20 yr ground-only, +1.2 K with a dry cooler (Zurmuhl 2018, small field); about +3 K in 3 yr where 4.8 × more heat went in than out (Kindaichi 2018, field measurement) — a borefield only lasts if neighbours take heat back out in winter

btes.f: heat out = η × heat stored; boreholes = charge W ÷ 47–83 W/m ÷ 35–55 m
btes.c: η 0.45 steady state (simulated), 0.32–0.56 measured years 3–10, 0.06–0.21 in years 1–2 (Drake Landing, Okotoks); a 0.9 MW data-centre design: 240 boreholes, 55 m deep, 3 m apart, 1,863 m², waste-heat use 77 → 96 %, ~17-yr payback (Li et al. 2021); heat-pump COP for the lift not given (gap)

ates.f: flow = MW × 3.6 ÷ (4.18 × ΔT); heat out ≈ 0.6 × heat in
ates.c: 172 m³/h per MW at ΔT 5 K (assumption); injection ≤25 °C typical (Netherlands limit; no BC/AB limit found) — air-cooled data-centre heat (25–35 °C) may exceed it; recovery 0.6 (0.4–0.85), ≈ €300/kW at 2 MW (Barth et al. 2026); BC: water licence (WSA); Alberta: Water Act approval or licence + professional report

deep_geo.c: Edmonton: ~90 °C at 2.5 km, 30–80 kg/s → 2.1–5.6 MWth average per well pair, $4.7–8 M per well (Majorowicz & Grasby 2021); licensed by the AER (Directive 089, 2025); competes with data-centre heat as a district source rather than cooling the data centre; Vancouver: not plausible for power, direct use unproven

tes_volume.c: 144 L/kWh at ΔT 6 K, 29 L/kWh at 30 K (physics); ice ≈ 10.5 kg per kWh; usable share 0.85 and tank heights are assumptions; costs too wide to use (IRENA range)

absorption.n: Cooling for neighbours from waste heat
absorption.f: cooling = recovered heat × COP, if temperature allows
absorption.c: 18 Oct 2026 (J.B. decisions, heat items 1–7; audit/heat_items_sources_2026-10-18.md): absorption ≥70–90 °C (single-effect ≥90, two-stage 70–80; Chen et al. 2026); adsorption from about 45–65 °C (LRZ CoolMUC-2 from 45 °C, operator; Meyer et al. 2013, ~65 °C, preprint). Air-cooled 25–47 °C: heat pump first (possible with a change); liquid-cooled 50–60 °C: adsorption possible, absorption with a heat pump. Earlier: single-effect absorption needs ≥90 °C, COP 0.6–0.7; two-stage 70–80 °C, COP <0.4 …

envelope.f: max floor area = site area × FSR (or FAR) available to the data-centre use; height, setbacks and building-width limits from the zone
envelope.c: Vancouver I-3 A: FSR 3.00 (bonus not open to storage uses), 18.3 m (30.5 m discretionary), side yard 7.6 m, max building width and depth 61.0 m, floor-to-floor ≥ 6.0 m ground / 4.0 m above; FC-2: FSR 1.00–5.00 by sub-area (6.50 at discretion), 10.7–22.9 m (to 51.8 m), side yards not permitted; I-2: FSR 3.00, 18.3 m (to 30.5–36.5 m); I-1C: FSR 6.00, 46.5 m. Vancouver counts plant floor space above grade (excluded only at or below base surface, e.g. I-2 s. 4.1.2(c)). Edmonton IM: 18.0 m, FAR 2.0, …
envelope.st: sourced for I-2, I-1C, I-3, FC-2, BE, IM, IH; FC-2 sub-area D bonus and E height unread; sub-area maps to digitise
envelope.w: what the zone lets it be

component_space.f: Σ components (electrical yard and switchgear, UPS and batteries, generators and fuel, heat rejection, heat recovery, fire suppression, loading) × IT load × redundancy
component_space.c: 18 Oct 2026 (sweep M30–M32; audit/plant_sources_2026-10-18.md): cooling space is per MW of HEAT (servers × PUE), spares added when the plant is laid out; air cooling → air-cooled chillers with free-cooling coils, 17–26 m²/MW (Trane TCA; a dry cooler cannot cool water below outdoor air, and air-cooled halls need ≥13 °C chilled water, NREL/DOE FEMP 2024); liquid cooling → dry coolers, 19.5–30.5 m²/MW (EVAPCO, Thermokey, Mark; manufacturer claims). Manufacturer claims per MW: UPS ≈2.0–2.4 m², …
component_space.st: manufacturer claims; clearances and switchgear room sizes unsourced

hall_area.f: new: envelope floor area − plant space − support − ground-floor uses the zone requires; part of an existing building: the floor area offered
hall_area.c: Vancouver I-2, I-3 and FC-2: no data storage at the ground floor except entrances; calibration: Burlington 3,710 m² of halls = 48–72 % of gross area
hall_area.st: arithmetic on sourced limits; white-space share from one calibration case

size_fit.f: hall area ÷ area per MW (range); for part of a building, also capped by floor load, electrical service and heat-rejection space
size_fit.c: LBNL prototypes 3.7–13.9 m² per rack → ≈186–2,325 m² per MW; Ark UP4 28 MW IT in 15,410 m² (three buildings); 111 E 5th ≤ 291 m² per MW (upper bound); Uptime 2024 average 8 kW per rack (industry survey)
size_fit.st: range, wide; narrows with rack density
size_fit.w: how big a data centre fits here

floor_load_need.f: equipment load of the hall (racks, batteries) vs the floor's design load for its original use
floor_load_need.c: NBC 2020 Table 4.1.5.3: office 2.4 kPa (upper floors), 4.8 kPa (basement and ground floors with exterior access); equipment and service rooms ≥ 3.6 kPa; office row excludes computer rooms; data halls designed for actual loads (4.1.5.1.(1)); data-hall values 7.2 kPa (US DoD) and 12 kPa (TIA-942 Rated-3) need the standard
floor_load_need.st: code values sourced; data-hall loads need the standard

fuel_on_site.f: generator capacity × runtime hours × fuel per kWh, against the limit per storage room for the storey it sits on
fuel_on_site.c: NFC 2020 Table 4.3.13.4.-B (Class II): first storey 200 000 L per room; basement or above the first storey 20 000 L (tanks > 2 500 L) or 45 000 L (tanks > 20 000 L); tanks > 230 L in a dedicated 2 h room; fuel use ≈0.263 L/kWh (one Cat model, manufacturer claim) ≈6.3 m³ per MW per 24 h; Uptime ≥ 12 h on site; whether data-centre standby counts as "emergency generators" is for the authority to decide
fuel_on_site.st: code limits sourced; fuel rate is a manufacturer claim
fuel_on_site.w: fuel kept on site: amount and type only, never location

flood_exposure.f: floor elevation of the plant vs the flood construction level, for parcels in the designated floodplain
flood_exposure.c: Vancouver FCL 4.6 m (GVRD datum, includes 1 m sea-level rise to 2100, 1:500-yr, 0.6 m freeboard); switchgear, electrical panels and fire protection not below FCL unless flood-protected (VBBL Div. C 2.2.9.3(2)); main switchgear in industrial buildings at or above FCL (F014 s. 3.3)
flood_exposure.u: m above or below the flood level
flood_exposure.st: Vancouver sourced; datum conversion not found; Edmonton not yet looked at

vibration_rank.f: qualitative rank of how hard plant vibration is to isolate at each position in the building
vibration_rank.c: NBC/VBBL apparent STC 47 between dwellings and other spaces (STC 55 by elevator shafts) — airborne only, no equipment-vibration limit; isolator deflection rises with floor span (US government spec citing ASHRAE); ASHRAE Applications ch. 49 not read
vibration_rank.u: ranked: slab on grade → long-span upper floor

service_class.f: IT load × PUE → the utility service class and what it brings (second feeder, transmission, clearances)
service_class.c: BC Hydro: above 6.5 MVA (12.5 kV areas) or 13 MVA (25 kV areas) a two-feeder supply may be required; 60 kV and above under transmission rules. EPCOR: primary service typical above 2,500 kVA; transformer clearances 3.0 m / 2.0 m; access road 4.6 m in a 6.5 m strip

receivers_nearby.f: every candidate receiver whose straight-line distance ≤ its type's reach (receiver_radius); each carries its demand (disclosed, else floor area × intensity), the temperature its type needs, its profile, and where the record came from
receivers_nearby.c: types: hot-water district network · ambient (low-temperature) network · steam network · pool · ice rink (also a source) · school · hospital or care home · housing · office · greenhouse · wastewater plant. Pools: water ≤ 37 °C by regulation, 25–28 °C recommended for competition pools (BC 2025). Ambient networks (Blatchford) take heat near ground temperature and lift it in each building. Hot water stored for taps must be at least 60 °C, and 49 °C anywhere in a recirculation loop (Vancouver …
receivers_nearby.u: list: type, distance, demand, temperature, evidence
receivers_nearby.st: data in hand (15 Oct); Vancouver pools and Edmonton care homes thin in the national records
receivers_nearby.w: buildings nearby that could use the heat

competing_sources.n: Other sources for the same receiver
competing_sources.f: sources already serving, or planned for, each receiver: sewage heat recovery, wastewater plants, ice-rink refrigeration, other data centres, ground loops; a receiver whose demand is already met by a low-carbon source is a weaker match, not a missing one
competing_sources.c: Vancouver NEU: 70% renewable, mostly sewage heat recovery, 6.6 MW added, 100% renewable target 2030 (City page, May 2025); Blatchford (Edmonton): ambient loop on geo-exchange and sewer heat. Ice rinks reject refrigeration heat — a source as well as a receiver. NEU By-law 9552 (2026): inside its service area, new buildings and major alterations must take NEU heat unless the City Engineer finds it not practical or economical (s. 2.1); heat returned to the network is credited at 50% of …
competing_sources.st: two networks sourced; others per receiver

displaced_source.f: the heat source a match would replace: from the host-building question (gas boilers · hot-water system · electric baseboard · district energy) or the network's supply mix; carbon change = displaced heat × its factor − heat-pump electricity × grid factor, which can be zero or negative where the …
displaced_source.c: factors from grid_co2 (NIR 2026) and the network's own reported mix; a network share described as "renewable" is the operator's word and is shown as such
displaced_source.st: logic defined; factors per network to source

hourly_overlap.f: for each hour of the typical year: delivered = min(heat available, receiver demand); report the share of the receiver's annual demand met, the heat still rejected (surplus), and the receiver's peak that must be met without the data centre
hourly_overlap.c: annual totals overstate the match: Vancouver heat demand is 47% in Dec–Feb and 2.5% in Jun–Aug (CWEC, computed); the data centre's heat is near-flat
hourly_overlap.u: % of receiver demand met · MWh surplus · MW backup

workload_control.f: flexible load is offered only by whoever runs the workloads: a single-owner or hyperscale operator can shift its own computing; in colocation the building operator controls power and cooling, not the tenants' computing, so flexibility needs each tenant's agreement
workload_control.c: business model from operator pages (claims) and permits; the learning-series EV and workload papers are models of single-operator fleets
workload_control.st: logic defined; per-site model from operator pages; Crozier & Liska 2025: no published flexible share — inference is inflexible, checkpointed training can pause

commitment.f: existing = operating; committed = in a contract, permit condition or funded budget; planned = in a utility filing or adopted plan; proposed = an applicant or operator says so; possible = the tool found it and nobody has proposed it. Only existing and committed count as delivered
commitment.c: states and rule set 14 Oct 2026 (learning-series critique); promised heat that is only possible is shown, never counted

futures.f: rerun the match in four futures: (1) as planned; (2) the tenant changes cooling — air ↔ liquid changes heat temperature, capture share and flexibility; (3) the tenant leaves — the receiver's backup carries its full peak and the building's reusable parts are listed; (4) the receiver leaves — all …
futures.c: lifespans from horizons (servers ~6 years, plant 15–25, network 40–50); closure cases in meta.lifecycle

property_tax.f: assessed value (land + taxable improvements) × combined class rate
property_tax.c: Vancouver Class 6 (Business & Other): 12.4672 per $1,000 in 2026, of which the City 7.09436; Edmonton non-residential: 25.22 + 3.97 education = 29.19 per $1,000 in 2026; servers and computing equipment are not municipally assessed in Alberta; in BC whether servers are assessed is not settled (0)
property_tax.st: rates read (90); the improvement value of a new building is assumed from its cost (60)

tax_split.f: list the parties, not a sum: City / school (Province) / TransLink and BC Assessment (Vancouver); City / education (Province) (Edmonton); then the City's spending shares
tax_split.c: Vancouver: property tax ≈ 56% of City operating revenue, utilities the largest spending share (24%), police second (22%); Edmonton: "where taxes go" page

untaxed_equipment.f: per city, list what is and is not taxed: shell and land (assessed), computing equipment (Alberta: not municipally assessed; ≥ 75 MW provincial levy), BC servers (not settled)
untaxed_equipment.c: Alberta Data Centre Levy from 1 Jan 2026 for ≥ 75 MW: (E + F) × R; E = 45% of cost of equipment under 4 years, F = 15% of older; R 2% on grid power → about 0.9% of new equipment cost a year; paid to the Province, creditable against Alberta corporate tax; Vancouver: no equivalent
untaxed_equipment.st: levy read from the bill (90); MGA side waits on Assessment Bulletin 25-02 (50)

computing_served.f: up to four sourced statements, no score: federal data-residency rule; provincial rule; the local internet exchange and its size; residency ≠ sovereignty
computing_served.c: Federal: Protected B and above stored in Canada; BC: data residency removed 2021, sensitive data abroad needs an assessment; Alberta: no rule found; Vancouver exchanges 158 participants across three, Edmonton YEGIX 9

afterlife.f: at closure, three streams: shell (reuse or demolition), equipment (stewardship program or disposal, with data sanitization), plant and batteries
afterlife.c: Vacated first-generation centres "tend to remain unoccupied and are not readily adaptable" (UK VOA, 70); federal closures 500+ of 720; BC Recycling Regulation covers IT products (servers by interpretation, 60); Alberta designates computer equipment; large UPS batteries outside both consumer programs as read (gap); no official source on converting a data centre to another use
afterlife.st: shell evidence transferred from the UK; conversion evidence a gap

heat_flux_site.n: Heat given off per m² of site
heat_flux_site.f: q = heat rejected at peak (W) ÷ site area (m²); shown beside the city value
heat_flux_site.c: Vancouver grid-cell anthropogenic heat flux 119 (units assumed W/m²; Allen et al. 2011); Edmonton: no published value; US city-wide fluxes 10–75 W/m², about 1 °C of air warming per 100 W/m² at neighbourhood scale (cited in Sailor 2026); check: 10 MW over 1 ha → 1,000 W/m²

heat_plume_dT.n: Warmer air near the cooling units
heat_plume_dT.f: at the coil: ΔT = Q ÷ (ρ·cp·airflow); at a neighbour: ΔT ≈ Q ÷ (ρ·cp) × (χ/Q)(x), the plume factor from air_screen_1h; heat treated as a passive tracer (buoyant rise ignored)
heat_plume_dT.c: airflow from manufacturer data (claim, 50); screening estimate, not a measured air temperature. Measured (first field study, Phoenix, 36–169 MW): downwind air 0.7–0.9 °C warmer on average, up to 2.2 °C, detectable 100–500 m away; condenser discharge 8–14 °C above ambient. Placement: units on the roof warm street-level air less than units on walls (Berlin model: up to 0.6 K for wall units, smaller for rooftop; Jin et al. 2020). The effect is strongest at night: Phoenix AC waste heat added more …
heat_plume_dT.st: physics at the coil (100); at a neighbour derived (60); field range peer-reviewed but transferred from large desert sites (70)
heat_plume_dT.w: warmer air near the cooling units

recirculation_flag.n: Warm air drawn back into the coolers
recirculation_flag.f: flag when the coolers sit inside a roof recirculation zone — top of the units below Hc = 0.22R near the upwind roof edge (R = Bs^0.67 × BL^0.33, Bs and BL the smaller and larger of the building's upwind height and width) — or within R downwind of a taller neighbour, or next to a wall or screen that …
recirculation_flag.c: wind alone cut a modelled bank's heat rejection to 83.5–89.5% of still-air (Duvenhage & Kröger 1996, peer-reviewed, numerical: cross wind starves up-wind fans; wind along the bank drives plume recirculation; higher fan platforms recirculate more); field cases 13.6% and 24% recirculation (1971, manufacturer engineers — claim); a hot roof warmed inlet air about 0.3 °C (Wray & Akbari 2008, 70); ASHRAE: recirculation "can be a serious problem" for units with intake and exhaust on one housing; roof …
recirculation_flag.st: geometric flag from the ASHRAE handbook (approximate); no recirculation percentage formula

uhi_context.f: one line per city: the City's heat policy and action, and the measured surface heat island
uhi_context.c: Vancouver: heat mapping, 30% canopy by 2050; Edmonton: Cool Edmonton (Action 9), hot days about 1 → 16 a year by the 2050s; surface heat island Vancouver summer day 7.25 °C, Edmonton winter night 2.86 °C (Duan et al. 2026); near data centres in Phoenix, surface about 0.5 °C warmer within 1 km and less vegetation, with low-income and minority neighbours over-represented (Molla 2026, exploratory, no causality); neither city regulates heat rejected by equipment

genset_emission_rate.f: Q = emission factor (g/kWh) × generator kWe × load ÷ 3,600
genset_emission_rate.c: NOx 14.6 g/kWh uncontrolled (AP-42 upper bound, as genset_test); check: 2,000 kWe at full load → 8.1 g/s (29.2 kg/h); generic equipment only

air_screen_1h.f: C(1 h) = 10⁶ × Q ÷ (π·u·σy·σz) × exp(−H² ÷ 2σz²); urban dispersion coefficients; u = 1 m/s, neutral class as a stated worst-case pick; preferred: AERSCREEN tables precomputed for three generic stacks
air_screen_1h.c: AERSCREEN is the screening tool in both provinces ("preferred" in BC, "recommended" in Alberta); label: screening — a regulator would require AERSCREEN or refined modelling; dispersion coefficient table to be checked against the final ISC3 edition

no2_at_receptor.f: NO2 = NOx at the receptor × conversion ratio: 1.0 (Tier 1) to the ARM2 bounds 0.9–0.2; diesel in-stack ratio 0.083
no2_at_receptor.c: BC NO2 guidance (2022); Edmonton uses Tier 1 only until Alberta Model Guideline s. 7.3 is read
no2_at_receptor.st: rule read (BC); Alberta numbers not read

air_vs_objective.f: C(avg) = C(1 h) × averaging ratio (24 h 0.60, annual 0.10) + background; test against the city objective AND the federal standard: "passes screen" or "refined modelling needed"; no score
air_vs_objective.c: Vancouver: Metro Vancouver NO2 1-h 79 µg/m³, annual 22.6; PM2.5 24-h 25; Clark Drive background NO2 ≈ 82 µg/m³ (1-h metric), already over the regional objectives; Edmonton: Alberta NO2 1-h 300 µg/m³ (hour by hour, reading 60), PM2.5 24-h 29; federal NO2 1-h 79 (2025), PM2.5 27 → 23 (2030); Edmonton short-term background a gap
air_vs_objective.w: air at neighbours against the limits

air_permit_trigger.f: Vancouver: daily NOx on a test day vs 5 kg/day (Bylaw 1082 s. 7(12)); Edmonton: emergency standby generators exempt from an EPEA approval
air_permit_trigger.c: a 2 MW generator at full load passes 5 kg of NOx in about 10 minutes (arithmetic, 60: whether s. 7(9) exempts engines outright is unsettled)
air_permit_trigger.w: whether an air permit is needed

free_cooling_hours_2050s.f: same count as free_cooling_hours, run on the PCIC 2050s file (SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5); shown beside today's value
free_cooling_hours_2050s.c: computed 19 Oct 2026 from the PCIC files (Vancouver Intl): hours ≤ 8 °C 3,284 now → 2,279 (SSP2-4.5) / 1,954 (SSP5-8.5); hours > 18 °C 1,085 → 1,879 / 2,218; peak 25.6 → 27.6 / 28.6 °C. Edmonton Intl: hours ≤ 8 °C 5,522 → 5,047 / 4,815; hours > 18 °C 914 → 1,259 / 1,479; hours ≥ 30 °C 0 → 22 / 71; peak 29.0 → 31.9 / 33.3 °C. Files shift averages ("Heat waves or cold spells remain largely unchanged")
free_cooling_hours_2050s.st: computed from the PCIC files (both cities, Intl stations, same method)

homes_heated_2050s.f: homes = heat available ÷ (space heat × HDD(2050s) ÷ HDD(now) + hot water)
homes_heated_2050s.c: space / hot-water split from CEUD 2023 (BC 46.2% / 27.1%; AB 63.1% / 23.2%); space heat assumed ∝ HDD, hot water unchanged; computed from PCIC (daily-mean HDD18): Vancouver 2,755 now → 2,198 (SSP2-4.5, −20%) / 2,038 (SSP5-8.5, −26%); Edmonton 5,389 → 4,659 (−14%) / 4,377 (−19%); published (RCP8.5, not like-for-like): Metro Vancouver −25%, Edmonton 5,657 → 4,331
homes_heated_2050s.w: homes its heat could warm in the 2050s

water_restriction_rule.f: per city, text only: what each restriction stage asks of evaporative cooling
water_restriction_rule.c: Vancouver: stages 1–3 do not restrict evaporative cooling; stage 4 asks industry for voluntary cuts; once-through cooling on City water banned at all times; towers need a permit and monthly Legionella reports. Edmonton: EPCOR stages target 5/10/15/25% cuts; stages 3–4 "must"; cooling towers reduced "where possible"; whether data-centre cooling is essential is not defined
water_restriction_rule.w: what a drought would ask of it

restriction_history.c: Vancouver: Stage 3 2015; Stage 2 2023 (4 Aug–15 Oct); 2026 Stage 3 from 8 Jun; Edmonton: one mandatory ban 29 Jan–2 Feb 2024 (plant failure, not drought); EPCOR: restrictions not every year

importance_cat.f: Normal (IE 1.0) by default; High (1.3) if likely used as a post-disaster shelter; post-disaster (1.5) if it serves as a communications facility, unless the authority exempts
importance_cat.c: High raises seismic design forces 30% over Normal (ratio only, not cost); Vancouver's new seismic rules apply to permits from 15 Sep 2026; whether a data centre counts as a communications facility is for the authority (20)

seismic_sa02.f: Sa(0.2) for the city; replace with the NRCan calculator value for the parcel
seismic_sa02.c: Vancouver 0.848, Edmonton 0.103 (proposed 2020 table; final table not read): Vancouver about 8×

refuge_after_quake.f: credible after an earthquake only if ALL: designed High or above; backup power serves the refuge space; group-lodging basics; local emergency services list it; otherwise "everyday heat, cold and smoke events only"
refuge_after_quake.c: BC: facilities "will only be opened up if they are suitable and have power"; Vancouver plans hubs around community centres (23 of 25); Edmonton opens warming spaces at −20 °C with wind chill for 3 days; neither city lists private or industrial buildings
refuge_after_quake.w: whether it could shelter people after an earthquake

battery_code_path.f: grid battery (ESS): certified; not above 23 m or below the lowest egress level unless in an electrical equipment vault; outdoors ≥ 3 m from egress and ≥ 1.5 m from openings unless UL 9540A-evaluated; UPS batteries are not an ESS and follow the general battery rules (ventilation, authorized access)
battery_code_path.c: CEC 2024 Section 64 (Rules 64-902, 64-926, 64-1002; Appendix B) in force BC 4 Mar 2025, Alberta 1 Apr 2025; no city fire bylaw adds battery rules in either city; NFPA 855 commercial thresholds stay reference only (unverified)

nations_named.f: the City's own wording, and links to each Nation's own referral page; no statement of any Nation's position
nations_named.c: Vancouver: xʷməθkʷəy̓əm (Musqueam), Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish), səlilwətaɬ (Tsleil-Waututh), unceded territories; Edmonton: Treaty 6 territory and the Métis homeland, peoples named, not individual Nations (Confederacy of Treaty No. 6 lists 15)

city_commitments.f: commitments, not legal duties: Vancouver UNDRIP Strategy Calls 1.18, 2.1–2.3, 2.5, 3.10 and the Action Plan engagement framework (in progress); Edmonton Indigenous Framework roles and Urban Reserve Strategy
city_commitments.c: Vancouver endorsed the Strategy 25 Oct 2022 and the Action Plan 25 Jun 2024; Edmonton has no land-use or rezoning commitment like Vancouver's (stated plainly)

vibration_target.f: compare with reference criteria: 72 VdB homes at night, 75 institutions, 65 vibration-sensitive rooms
vibration_target.c: US FTA criteria, transferred; neither city's noise bylaw mentions vibration; ISO standards set no neighbour limits

embodied_rule.f: Vancouver: new buildings at most 2× the baseline (800 kg CO2e/m² on the absolute path, our calculation); Edmonton: no requirement for private buildings

heat_value_split.n: Who keeps the value of the heat
heat_value_split.f: describe who controls each share (operator, utility, end users); no numeric split
heat_value_split.c: no study measures the split; peer-reviewed papers say it is negotiated and the utility holds the stronger hand; a numeric split stays a gap (0) — a gap the thesis could fill
heat_value_split.w: who keeps the value of the heat

power_bill_effect.f: by size and province, text only: a typical in-city data centre (≈ 2.5 MW) shows no measurable effect in any source; very large loads depend on provincial connection policy
power_bill_effect.c: BC Hydro modelling (2026): one new 75–250 MVA customer changes all rates by +0.4 to +1.5% by F2036 with no threshold, 0 to −1.2% under threshold options; AESO (2025): whether large loads pay their fair share of transmission costs is still open; LBNL (2025): mechanisms and protections, no quantified effect
